title: Damped Oscillation
short: Multiply a sinusoid by a decaying exponential.

blocks.html: A plucked guitar string or a car bouncing on its springs oscillates, but each swing is smaller than the last. To model that, keep a sinusoid for the back-and-forth and multiply it by a decaying exponential for the shrinking size.

$$y = Ae^{-kt}\cos(\omega t) \quad (k > 0)$$ oscillates with period $\frac{2\pi}{\omega}$ between the curves $y = Ae^{-kt}$ and $y = -Ae^{-kt}$, called the envelope. Any decay factor works the same way, such as $A\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^t\cos(\omega t)$.

Because $-1 \le \cos(\omega t) \le 1$, multiplying by $Ae^{-kt}$ gives $-Ae^{-kt} \le y \le Ae^{-kt}$. The graph touches the top of the envelope wherever $\cos(\omega t) = 1$ and the bottom wherever it is $-1$, and crosses zero wherever cosine does, so the timing of the swings does not change. Only their size shrinks.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Set $k = 0$ and the swings never shrink. Raise $k$ and the dashed envelope closes in faster.

blocks.title: A value
steps: $\cos(6\pi) = 1$, so the point is on the top of the envelope.

blocks.title: Writing a model
blocks.q: A mass starts $10$ cm above its rest position, oscillates with period $2$ seconds, and its swings decay like $e^{-0.3t}$. Write $y(t)$.
steps: At $t = 0$ it is at its highest, so use cosine with $A = 10$.

blocks.title: When is it small?
blocks.q: For $y = 16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^t\cos(\pi t)$, when has the envelope shrunk to $1$?
steps: So $t = 4$. After that every swing is less than $1$ in size.

blocks.html: Adding the exponential instead of multiplying. $y = \cos t + e^{-t}$ just slides the midline as the exponential fades; the swings stay the same size. Check: in a damped model, the distance between a peak and the next trough must shrink.
